content: Eczema and food allergies are prevalent health issues that often begin in early childhood and frequently coexist in the same individuals. These conditions are thought to be associated with an impaired skin barrier during early infancy. It remains uncertain whether interventions aimed at preventing or repairing an impaired skin barrier shortly after birth are effective in reducing the risk of eczema or food allergies. The primary goal of this research was to evaluate the effects of skin care interventions, such as the use of emollients, on the primary prevention of eczema and food allergies in infants. A secondary objective was to identify specific characteristics of study populations, such as age, genetic predisposition, and adherence to interventions, that might influence the effectiveness or potential harm of these interventions. To address these objectives, a comprehensive search was conducted in September 2021 across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Skin Specialised Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and Embase. Additional searches of trial registries and conference proceedings were performed to identify relevant randomized controlled trials (RCTs). The inclusion criteria focused on RCTs involving skin care interventions designed to enhance skin barrier function, reduce dryness, or mitigate subclinical inflammation in healthy, full-term infants (born at ≥37 weeks of gestation) under 12 months of age, without pre-existing eczema, food allergies, or other skin conditions. Comparisons were made against standard care or no treatment, and no minimum follow-up duration was required. The analysis was conducted as a prospective individual participant data (IPD) meta-analysis, following standard Cochrane methodological procedures. The primary outcomes assessed were the cumulative incidence of eczema and immunoglobulin E (IgE)-mediated food allergies by one to three years of age, measured at the closest available time point to two years. Secondary outcomes included adverse events during the intervention period, clinician-assessed eczema severity, parent-reported eczema severity, time to eczema onset, parent-reported immediate food allergy, and allergic sensitization to food or inhalant allergens. A total of 33 RCTs involving 25,827 participants were identified, with 17 studies (5,823 participants) reporting data on one or more outcomes of interest. Eleven studies (5,217 participants) were included in one or more meta-analyses, with 10 of these providing IPD. The remaining six studies were included in the narrative synthesis only. Most studies were conducted in pediatric hospital settings. Twenty-five studies, including all those contributing to meta-analyses, involved newborns up to three weeks of age who were randomized to receive a skin care intervention or standard care. Eight of the 11 studies contributing to meta-analyses recruited infants at high risk of developing eczema or food allergies, though the definition of high risk varied across studies. The duration of interventions and follow-up ranged from 24 hours to three years. The majority of the evidence was assessed as low certainty, with concerns about potential bias. These concerns were primarily due to a lack of blinding among outcome assessors and significant missing data, which could have influenced the results but were judged unlikely to have done so. The evidence for the primary food allergy outcome was considered to have a high risk of bias, as it was based on a single trial with findings that varied depending on assumptions about missing data. The findings suggest that skin care interventions during infancy likely do not reduce the risk of eczema by one to three years of age (risk ratio [RR] 1.03, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.81 to 1.31; moderate-certainty evidence). Similarly, these interventions likely do not affect the time to eczema onset (hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.14; moderate-certainty evidence). However, skin care interventions may increase the risk of IgE-mediated food allergies by one to three years of age (RR 2.53, 95% CI 0.99 to 6.49; low-certainty evidence), although they may not alter the risk of allergic sensitization to food allergens (RR 1.05, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.71; low-certainty evidence). Additionally, these interventions may slightly increase the risk of parent-reported immediate reactions to common food allergens at two years of age (RR 1.27, 95% CI 1.00 to 1.61; low-certainty evidence), though this was primarily observed for cow’s milk and may be unreliable due to potential over-reporting of milk allergies in infants. Skin care interventions during infancy likely increase the risk of skin infections during the intervention period (RR 1.33, 95% CI 1.01 to 1.75; moderate-certainty evidence). They may also increase the risk of infant slippage (RR 1.42, 95% CI 0.67 to 2.99; low-certainty evidence) and stinging or allergic reactions to moisturizers (RR 2.24, 95% CI 0.67 to 7.43; low-certainty evidence), although the confidence intervals for these outcomes were wide and included the possibility of no effect or reduced risk. Preplanned subgroup analyses indicated that the effects of skin care interventions on eczema risk were not influenced by factors such as age, duration of intervention, hereditary risk, filaggrin (FLG) mutation, chromosome 11 intergenic variant rs2212434, or the classification of intervention type. However, the effects of these factors on food allergy risk could not be evaluated due to insufficient evidence. Additionally, there was insufficient evidence to determine whether adherence to interventions influenced the relationship between skin care interventions and the development of eczema or food allergies. In conclusion, based on lowto moderate-certainty evidence, skin care interventions such as emollients during the first year of life in healthy infants are unlikely to prevent eczema, may increase the risk of food allergies, and likely increase the risk of skin infections. Further research is needed to explore whether alternative approaches to infant skin care could effectively prevent eczema or food allergies.
